content.title: Home insurance rates by state for April 2026
content.text: Written by Edited by Updated Feb 26, 2026 Find quotes for your area Location Pin Icon Explore offers from trusted carriers + MORE Homeowners insurance rates by state If you live in Florida, you probably worry about your roof and windows when big storms blow in. Homeowners in Oklahoma keep a close eye on tornado forecasts, and Californians might carve out time each spring to clear away brush in their yards in case of summer wildfires. You're aware of the regional risks to your home, and so is your insurer. That's why homes in riskier areas cost more to insure. Home insurance rates have risen in many states due to increases in extreme weather, inflation, supply chain challenges (for sourcing repair materials) and insurance fraud. Fortunately, legislative and carrier action in problematic states seems to finally be turning the tide on skyrocketing premiums. "Florida’s state-backed insurer of last resort, Citizens Property Insurance Corp., has shed more than 1 million policies over the past two years due to depopulation to the vastly improved private market," says Mark Friedlander, director of corporate communications for the Insurance Information Institute (Triple-I). "Florida’s home insurance industry is forecast to post its second consecutive underwriting profit in 2025, after nearly a decade of significant annual underwriting losses." There are positive signs in Louisiana, where the 2020/21 hurricane season threw the home insurance market into turmoil, causing a dozen insurers to go insolvent or stop writing new policies in the state. "We are also starting to see premium relief in Louisiana following legislative reform measures passed in 2024," says Friedlander. Unfortunately, not all home insurance markets are experiencing this turnaround. Friedlander notes: "Several Midwest states that experienced significant convective storm activity in 2025 are seeing substantial rate hikes. Convective storms accounted for more than $50 billion in U.S. insured losses in 2025, the third consecutive year above $50 billion in incurred losses for this peril." Knowing both the national average and how the average rate in your state compares could be useful baselines while shopping for home insurance. The map and table below shows homeowners insurance rates by state and the percentage of income spent, giving a quick view of how your state compares to others. Keep in mind that while flooding is a concern in many states, flood insurance is not part of standard homeowners policies. If you live in an area at risk for flooding, you will need to purchase a separate flood insurance policy. Earthquakes are also a common homeowners insurance exclusion. Like floods, earthquake damage must be covered by a separate policy. No U.S. landfalls during the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season was a key factor in the industry’s positive homeowners financial performance in 2025. Triple-I forecasts a slightly profitable 99.6 combined ratio for the homeowners sector in 2025, despite the record-level insured loss from the January 2025 Los Angeles fires.
